headline: 'They're paid by enemies of our nation': Trump lashes out at protesters amid Texas rally interruptions
content: US President Donald Trump was repeatedly interrupted by protesters during a campaign rally in San Antonio, Texas, on Wednesday (October 7) as he sought to rally support for Republican Senate nominee Ken Paxton. Several demonstrators heckled Trump during his remarks at the packed Freeman Coliseum, prompting security personnel and police to remove them from the venue. At least 10 protesters were ejected, with some incidents also involving clashes between demonstrators and rally attendees. Trump responded angrily to the interruptions, accusing the protesters of being paid by "enemies of our nation". Get the hell out of here, Trump told protesters as the disruptions continued. At one point, Trump briefly stepped away from the microphone as the uproar in the crowd grew. The interruptions occurred while he was criticizing Paxtons Democratic opponent, James Talarico, according to The Associated Press. Trump continued to address the demonstrators even as security repeatedly escorted them out. Hes going back home to mom, Trump said of one protester. But what he doesnt know is his mom voted for Trump. The President also mocked some of those removed from the rally, commenting on their appearance and weight. One has got to lose a lot of weight, Trump said, while describing others as really bad-looking people. Video from inside the venue showed some Trump supporters confronting protesters as they were being removed. In one incident, an attendee appeared to grab another man by the hair. The repeated disruptions forced Trump to pause or break from his remarks several times before continuing his speech. The rally was not focused entirely on the Texas Senate race. Trump also revisited controversial remarks he made earlier in the week about the possibility of Iran targeting US cities. Trump had previously suggested that Iran could try to take out Los Angeles and San Diego, comments that drew criticism from California officials. At the San Antonio rally, Trump repeated the warning while arguing that the United States would protect the cities. And I said it the other day, let them hit a missile into San Diego or Los Angeles on the way, Trump said. You want to see a horror show? Let them hit San Diego. Let them hit Los Angeles, he added. Were not going to let that happen. We protect our cities. We protect our country. The White House had defended Trump's earlier remarks, arguing that the cities were safe because the US had prevented Iran from developing a nuclear weapon. Trump's main political objective in San Antonio was to bolster Paxton, who is facing Talarico in a closely watched Senate contest. Trump described Paxton as perhaps the greatest attorney general in the United States of America and praised him for remaining loyal to the president. He was tough and he was with us all the way, Trump said. Hes a fantastic man. Paxton later joined Trump onstage and thanked the president for appearing at the rally. Trump repeatedly attacked Talarico, including over the death penalty, an issue with particular resonance in Texas, which leads the US in executions. Trump reiterated his support for the death penalty for large scale drug dealers, human traffickers and anyone who kills a police officer. He also referred to the execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, the former Army major convicted of killing 13 people in the 2009 Fort Hood mass shooting. Trump said Hasan would be executed by firing squad after he approved that method earlier this week. The rally came as Republicans devote increasing resources to Texas ahead of the November 3 midterm elections. Texas has long been one of the country's most reliably Republican states, with Trump winning it by nearly 14 percentage points in 2024. But Republicans are facing a more challenging political environment this year amid Trump's low approval ratings, the Iran war and rising fuel prices. A Reuters/Ipsos poll released Monday put Trump's approval rating at 32%, matching the lowest level recorded in the poll. Wednesday's appearance was Trump's third trip to Texas in less than a month to campaign for Paxton. Republican officials have it more than $300 million to elections in the state. The President's political standing was also underscored by the absence of Republican Governor Greg Abbott from the rally. Abbott, who won reelection in 2022 by about 11 percentage points, is himself facing a competitive reelection contest against Democratic state Representative Gina Hinojosa. Trump also used the rally to announce that retired baseball pitcher Roger Clemens would receive the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the nation's highest civilian honour. Trump called the award a step up from Clemens' failure to gain entry into the Baseball Hall of Fame.

headline: Monsoon withdrawal advances as India records one of its weakest seasons in decades
content: west monsoon is steadily pulling back from India, with the India Meteorological Department (IMD) saying on Thursday that conditions are now favourable for its withdrawal from more parts of the country over the next three to four days. The retreat follows a weak monsoon season, with cumulative rainfall 13% below the long-period average, amid developing El Nio conditions over the equatorial Pacific that are expected to intensify through year-end. India last recorded a below-normal monsoon in 2023, when rainfall was 95% of the long period average (LPA). The monsoon current has further withdrawn from the remaining areas of Maharashtra, parts of Goa, Karnataka, Telangana and Odisha, along with additional areas of Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh. Conditions are increasingly favourable for the monsoon to retreat from more parts of eastern India, the northern peninsula and large parts of north-east India over the next three to four days, the IMD said. The south-west monsoon typically begins withdrawing from western Rajasthan in September, before moving across northwest and central India and then toward the southern peninsula and eastern regions. The retreat does not mean an immediate end to rainfall. The IMD has forecast fairly widespread to widespread rain over Sub-Himalayan West Bengal and Sikkim on 9 October. Bihar is likely to receive rainfall during 9-11 October, while Odisha could see isolated to scattered rain through 14 October. In the north-east, rainfall is expected over Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Meghalaya and Nagaland, Manipur, Mizoram and Tripura over the coming days. Withdrawal is also progressing across the northern peninsula, with the monsoon already retreating from parts of Maharashtra, Goa, Karnataka and Telangana. Rainfall will nevertheless persist over parts of southern India, particularly Kerala, Tamil Nadu and Karnataka. The IMD has forecast isolated heavy rainfall over south interior Karnataka on 9 October, and over Kerala and Tamil Nadu, Puducherry and Karaikal during 9-10 October. In northwest India, scattered rainfall is expected over Haryana, Chandigarh, Delhi and Punjab during 9-14 October, while parts of Uttar Pradesh could receive rain through 11 October. The continued withdrawal marks the seasonal shift toward the northeast monsoon, even as rainfall remains active across parts of eastern, northeastern and southern India. Also Read | Monsoon withdrawal begins from western Rajasthan The south-west monsoon contributes about 70% of India's annual rainfall and is crucial for farm output, reservoir levels and the rural economy. South-west monsoon rainfall in 2026 stood at 87% of the LPA, with cumulative precipitation of 759.4 mm during the June-September season, making it the fourth-lowest since 2001 and the 13th-lowest since 1901, according to the IMD. India last recorded a below-normal monsoon in 2023, when rainfall was 95% of the LPA. Rainfall was below normal across most regions. South Peninsular India recorded just 76% of its LPA, with 542.0 mm of rainfall, making it the region's fourth-lowest monsoon rainfall since 1901 and second-lowest since 2001. Central India, by contrast, received normal rainfall at 97% of LPA. North-western India recorded 94.1% of LPA, while Northeast India received 74%.

headline: Loud Explosions Heard In Riyadh, Houthis Claim They Fired Missile At Airport
content: Several explosions were heard in Saudi Arabias capital Riyadh, with a major blast reported at King Khalid International Airport as Houthi attacks raise regional tensions. Several explosions were heard across Saudi Arabias capital Riyadh on Thursday, with a major blast reported near King Khalid International Airport, according to a witness who spoke to The Associated Press. The Iran-backed Houthi rebels later claimed responsibility, saying they had targeted the airport with a ballistic missile. The claim came after the Saudi-led coalition fighting the group said it had intercepted two missiles fired towards the Saudi capital. - Pakistan Expands Military Footprint In Saudi Arabia As Houthi Conflict Escalates | Exclusive - Pakistan Plans To Deploy Up To 25,000 Troops In Saudi Arabia Amid Rising Houthi Threat | Exclusive - From Riyadh Airport To Aramco Refinery: Yemen's Houthis Claim Strikes Across Saudi Arabia - Saudi Says Airport Attacks In Riyadh, Abha Kill 3, Injure 36 After Houthis Claim Strikes Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group had targeted King Khalid International Airport around midday, claiming that one of its ballistic missiles hit its target". The claim could not be independently verified. Flights Halted At Riyadh Airport King Khalid International Airport was reportedly closed again following the explosions. Flight-tracking service Flightradar24 said on X that the airport had recorded no recent arrivals or departures. A witness at the airport said fire and ambulance crews were deployed and smoke could be seen in the area. Outgoing flights were halted, while passengers were reportedly asked to leave their checked-in luggage and evacuate the airport. The extent of the disruption was not immediately clear. Saudi authorities had not responded to requests for comment. Houthis Claim Fresh Strike On Saudi Capital The latest incident comes amid a series of attacks claimed by the Houthis against Saudi targets in recent days. The group has repeatedly claimed strikes on airports, military installations and oil facilities in the kingdom. The Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted two missiles launched towards Riyadh on Thursday. The Houthis, however, said one missile targeting King Khalid International Airport had reached its intended target. The developments come a day after Saudi authorities reported attacks on two airports that killed three people and injured dozens. The attack on King Khalid airport killed a Sudanese national and wounded eight others, while a separate strike on Abha airport killed Moroccan and Algerian residents and injured 28 people, according to Saudi officials. The latest attacks have raised fresh security concerns in Saudi Arabia, the worlds largest oil exporter, as the kingdom becomes increasingly drawn into the wider regional conflict. Saudi Offensive Adds To Regional Tensions The attacks come after Saudi Arabia and allied Yemeni forces launched a major air and ground offensive against the Houthis over the weekend. The operation is aimed at retaking territory along Yemens western Red Sea coast and around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait that the rebels seized about a month ago. The Houthis presence around the strategic waterway has also raised concerns over international shipping. The Bab el-Mandeb is a key alternative route to the Strait of Hormuz, where maritime traffic has been disrupted amid the ongoing Iran war. On Wednesday, Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki, spokesperson for the Saudi-led coalition, said coalition forces had destroyed a launch platform in Yemens rebel-held capital, Sanaa, which was allegedly being used to launch attacks on Riyadh. Loud explosions were heard across Riyadh after the Iran-backed Houthi rebels targeted King Khalid International Airport with a ballistic missile. While the Saudi-led coalition stated it intercepted incoming missiles, Houthi officials claimed a missile hit its intended target, leading to flight disruptions and the evacuation of the airport.

headline: Youth held under Pocso Act for threatening schoolgirl near Tiruttani
content: Sindhu Kannan / Oct 08, 2026, 18:41 IST Chennai: A 19-year-old youth was arrested under the Pocso Act for threatening a schoolgirl near Tiruttani, demanding that she persuade her elder sister to accept his love proposal.Gopal, 19, intercepted the Class X student when was walking home from the bus stand after school, said police. He threatened her and demanded that she convince her elder sister, a Class XI student, to accept his proposal.The younger girl subsequently informed her parents about the incident. Following a complaint by her mother, Tiruttani All Women Police registered a case under the Pocso Act and arrested Gopal.

headline: Woman, son burned by boiling water amid property dispute
content: A woman and her 15-year-old son suffered severe burns after their relative poured boiling water on them during a property dispute at a village near RK Pet in Tiruttani.Murugan, a mason from Sellathur village, and his elder brother Devaraj, 40, a vegetable vendor, had been involved in a property dispute for some time. On Wednesday night, an argument broke out between the two families over the property. As the quarrel escalated, Devarajs wife Thangam brought boiling water drained from cooked rice and poured it on Murugans wife Seetha, and son Yuvaraj.Both suffered severe burns. Neighbours rushed them to a primary health centre for first aid. They were subsequently referred to Sholinghur Government Hospital before being shifted to Tiruvallur Government Medical College Hospital for further treatment.Based on complaints lodged by both families, RK Pet police registered cases and are investigating.

headline: Puducherry, Assam by-election results 2026 date and time: How to check Thattanchavady, Nagaon results online
content: Election Results 2026: The results of the by-elections to Puducherrys Thattanchavady Assembly constituency and Assams Nagaon Lok Sabha constituency will be declared on Friday, October 9. The vote counting will begin at 8 am at designated centres. The by-elections were held on October 6, alongside polling for by-elections in other states. Postal ballots will be counted first, followed by votes recorded through electronic voting machines (EVMs). The final result for each constituency will be declared after counting is completed and the Returning Officer certifies the result. The bypoll in Thattanchavady is being seen as a test of the popularity of the four-month-old NDA government led by veteran N Rangasamy. Although 11 candidates are in the fray, the contest is being viewed as a three-cornered battle between the ruling AINRC-led NDA, the Congress and its former ally, the DMK. AINRC founder and Chief Minister Rangasamy has nominated Ashok Anand on behalf of the ruling party and the coalition it leads. The Congress has fielded E Vinayagam, who has the backing of Tamizhaga Vetri Kazhagam (TVK), which is part of the ruling alliance in neighbouring Tamil Nadu. The DMK nominee is K Sedhu Selvam. CPIs M A Saleem and S Karthikumari of actor-politician Seemans Naam Tamilar Katchi are also among the candidates. The Nagaon Lok Sabha seat witnessed a triangular contest, with the ruling BJP seeking to expand its base in the Muslim-majority constituency, while the Congress is seeking to retain the seat by keeping its minority support base intact. The AIUDF, the third prominent party in the fray, is looking to maintain its influence after its tally was reduced to two MLAs from 16 in the April Assembly election. A total of 15 candidates, including nine Independents, are contesting the bypoll. Key candidates include former Congress MLA Sibamoni Bora, former IAS officer Devasish Sharma of the BJP and sitting MLA Badruddin Ajmal of the AIUDF. The bypoll was necessitated after sitting MP Pradyut Bordoloi quit the Congress to join the BJP ahead of the Assembly elections earlier this year.

headline: Goodbye 'Truck Shakedowns', Hello 3-Day Refunds: The 10 Biggest Reliefs In GST 2.0
content: Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman unveiled critical decisions and policy changes from the 57th GST Council meeting in New Delhi on October 8 Following the 57th GST Council meeting in New Delhi on October 8, Union Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman announced a decisive shift towards GST 2.0". With tax rate structures now fully settled and generating robust revenues, the Council has turned its complete focus towards eliminating administrative friction, protecting genuine taxpayers, and improving ease of doing business across the country. Here are the 10 most critical decisions and policy changes unveiled by the Finance Minister: - GST Council's New Goods-In-Transit Rules: Who Can Stop, Check And Seize Your Consignment? - GST Notices For Dues Below Rs. 10,000 Scrapped: What The New Rule Means For Taxpayers - GST Council Scraps Tax Officers Arrest Power, Raises Prosecution Limit To Rs. 5 Crore - Power Of Arrest Removed, No Double Taxation, Faster Refunds: GST Council Unveils Mega Reforms 1. Total Scrapping of Arrest Powers and Decriminalisation In a landmark move to curb tax harassment, the GST Council has completely removed the power of arrest from GST law. Furthermore, the monetary threshold for criminal prosecution has been quadrupled from Rs. 1 crore to Rs. 5 crore. Minimum mandatory punishments have been abolished, leaving penalties entirely to judicial discretion, while the general penalty for minor technical infractions has been cut from Rs. 25,000 to Rs. 10,000. 2. Big Relief for Small E-Commerce Sellers Small sellers will no longer need physical offices in every state to sell across India on digital platforms. Merchants with monthly tax liability below Rs. 2.5 lakh can now declare an e-commerce operators regional warehouse as their principal place of business. This single decision opens up nationwide pan-India markets to nearly 9.5 lakh small sellers without adding administrative overhead. 3. Protection and Relief for Genuine Buyers The 57th GST Council meeting was held in New Delhi on October 8. The power of arrest has been completely removed from GST law. The monetary threshold for criminal prosecution has been quadrupled from Rs. 1 crore to Rs. 5 crore. Small sellers with monthly tax liability below Rs. 2.5 lakh can now declare an e-commerce operators regional warehouse as their principal place of business. The time limit for issuing an official acknowledgement for refunds drops from 15 days to 10 days. Addressing a long-standing grievance, the Council established a dedicated Committee of Officers to safeguard honest buyers facing Input Tax Credit (ITC) denial due to supplier default. If a buyer holds a valid invoice, has received the goods, and paid the supplier in full, their credit will be protected. The committee will submit its binding framework within three months. 4. Major Unlocking of Capital: ITC on Machinery & Capital Goods Businesses subject to inverted duty structures will now be eligible to claim cash refunds on input services starting 1st November 2026. Additionally, the exclusion of capital goods from refunds has been lifted; tax paid on plant and machinery can now be recovered over a 60-month operational lifecycle starting 1st April 2027, releasing vast working capital for FMCG, manufacturing, and pharma sectors. 5. End to Arbitrary Highway Interceptions Transit inspections are being strictly overhauled. Transit goods can no longer be stopped routinely or checked in every state along a route. Moving forward, conveyances may only be inspected at the origin state or the destination state, and physical checks can only occur based on pre-authorised intelligence approved by an officer of Joint Commissioner rank or higher. 6. Accelerated Automated Refunds Refund timelines are being cut drastically. The time limit for issuing an official acknowledgement drops from 15 days to 10 days, failing which the system automatically acknowledges the claim. High-tech automated risk assessments will now clear and sanction 90% of low-risk refund claims within three working days, while excess cash ledger refunds will become 100% automated with zero human officer intervention. 7. Expanded Input Tax Credit on Ordinary Business Spending The Council has expanded ITC eligibility to cover essential business expenses previously blocked under strict tax rules. Businesses can now claim full credit on health and life insurance premiums paid for employees, telecommunication towers, external pipelines laid outside factory premises, free promotional samples, and expired stocks required by law to be destroyed. 8. Simplified Annual Filing for MSMEs An optional, highly simplified scheme was approved in principle for small consumer-facing taxpayers with annual turnovers up to Rs. 5 crore. Eligible small businesses will pay tax on a quarterly basis but will only need to file a tax return once a year, reducing compliance friction for over 16 lakh small enterprises. 9. Boost for IT and Service Exports To put Indian service exporters on an equal global footing, Indian firms operating through overseas branches will now seamlessly receive export benefits without regulatory hurdles. Furthermore, back-office processing, testing, and research conducted in India on foreign-owned goods will count as an official export of service, even if the physical goods do not leave Indian shores. 10. Lock-in on Annual Rate Reviews Signalling complete rate stability, no tax rates were altered during the meeting. The Finance Minister announced that future rate adjustments will no longer happen on a piecemeal basis; rate rationalisations will occur strictly once a year during a single dedicated Council meeting, giving corporate India complete predictability for long-term financial budgeting. The GST Council completely removed the power of arrest from GST law and quadrupled the monetary threshold for criminal prosecution from Rs. 1 crore to Rs. 5 crore. Additionally, minimum mandatory punishments have been abolished, leaving penalties to judicial discretion.

headline: Mint Explainer: What do we know about Russia's suspected plague outbreak?
content: Hundreds of people in Siberia have been quarantined after a laboratory worker at a plague research institute died in undisclosed circumstances on Friday. A Russian news outlet reported the woman may have contracted pneumonic plague from a broken test tube, a narrative that Russian health authorities have denied. As global health bodies and governments seek more information, Russia has said that the workers death does not risk an epidemic in Siberia. However, public health experts are vigilant, given the limited information available.

content: Viduthalai Chiruthaigal Katchi (VCK) leader Thol. Thirumavalavan on Wednesday said the INDIA blocs protest in New Delhi should evolve into a peoples movement against electronic voting machines (EVMs). headline: 'Can't examine allegations like a court conducting trial': J&K court slams police for delay in FIR
content: Coming down heavily on police for not registering a complaint in the case of a man whose body was found hanging from a tree in June, a local court in Jammu and Kashmirs Reasi district has said the force owes a duty to promptly register an FIR and initiate investigation in a case. The court said when an informant apprises the police regarding the commission of a cognizable offence, police authorities are not vested with any discretion to conduct a preliminary inquiry to assess the credibility of the information. Any such practice would be contrary to the established principles of criminal law, said Chief Judicial Magistrate, Reasi, Geeta Kumari, in her 12-page judgment, last week. Earlier, advocate M Zulkarnain Chowdhary, counsel for the brother of the deceased, told the court that police had not registered any case despite written complaints in the matter. The matter pertained to the death of a man whose body was found hanging from a tree near the house of the parents of his estranged wife on June 24. Despite a written complaint by the deceaseds brother, alleging that he had matrimonial discord with his wife, and that she along with her son had attacked him with an axe earlier as well, police initiated inquest proceedings in the matter instead of filing an FIR. The petitioner had sought registration of an FIR against 10 people, including his brothers wife and her son, alleging that they had called the deceased to attend a meeting and killed him after he refused to grant her a divorce. They later hanged his body from a tree to make it look like a case of suicide, he alleged. Making it clear that police cannot examine allegations levelled by the applicant as if the court is conducting a trial, the CJM directed the police to register an FIR in the matter. The question, presently, is whether the facts disclosed in the application prima facie indicate commission of a cognizable offence requiring investigation by the police. Referring to the inquest proceedings initiated by the police in the matter, the judge observed that these have a very limited scope. The object of these proceedings is merely to ascertain whether a person has died under suspicious circumstances, or an unnatural death and if so, what is the apparent cause of death, the CJM said. The question regarding the details as to how the deceased was assaulted, or by whom, or under what circumstances is foreign to the ambit and scope of the proceedings under Section 174 CrPC, she added. These inquest proceedings are distinct from those initiated after the registration of an FIR, the court said. The proceedings commence with the recording of an information pertaining to commission of a cognizable offence, the judge observed. Any step taken by the investigating officer pursuant to recording of such an information towards detection of the crime would be a part of investigation under the CrPC, she added. Pointing out that these are two distinct types of proceedings, the judge observed that inquest proceedings relate to ascertainment of apparent cause of death of a person who has died under mysterious circumstances, whereas proceedings pertaining to investigation relate to detection of the crime and all attending matters, including the apprehension of the culprits.

headline: Ayodhya's Ram Mandir to get FSSAI 'Eat Right Place' tag, says report; here's how the certification works
content: The Ram Temple in Ayodhya is set to receive the Eat Right Place recognition from the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI), according to a News18 report. This comes on the heels of an evaluation of the food safety, hygiene and quality standards maintained for prasad distributed and sold within the temple premises. The Eat Right Places of Worship (PoW) initiative by the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) seeks to improve food safety and hygiene standards at religious institutions. Under the programme, temples, gurdwaras, mosques and other places of worship are encouraged to adopt safe practices while preparing and serving prasad, langar and other food. A place of worship seeking Eat Right Place of Worship/BHOG recognition must first have a valid FSSAI registration or licence under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. The premises or relevant food handlers must meet the applicable regulatory requirements. The institution then undergoes a pre-audit, which involves checking its food safety practices against the hygiene requirements prescribed by FSSAI. Food handlers and cooks are also required to undergo training through FSSAI-empanelled partners under the Food Safety Training and Certification (FoSTaC) programme. The training covers the Basic Catering Course and focuses on safe food handling practices. After this, an FSSAI-recognised auditing agency conducts a third-party inspection of areas such as kitchens, storage facilities and food-serving spaces. Any shortcomings identified during the audit must be addressed through corrective measures. Once the required food safety and hygiene standards are fulfilled, the place of worship receives the BHOG certification under the Eat Right Place of Worship initiative. The Eat Right Place of Worship certificate is valid for two years from the date of issue. Meanwhile, the Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA) in August levied a 1 lakh fine on Amazon Seller Services, the marketplace arm of e-commerce major Amazon, for allegedly permitting the sale of sweets carrying the misleading description Shri Ram Mandir Ayodhya Prasad. "The CCPA hereby imposes a penalty of 1,00,000/- on the opposite party (Amazon Seller) for publication of misleading advertisements on its platform," in violation of the E-Commerce Rules, 2020, the CCPA said in an order passed on August 4 this year, according to PTI. The authority also directed Amazon Seller Services to ensure that "no product falsely claiming to be 'prasad', 'prasadam', 'mahaprasad', 'bhog' or any similarreligious offering" linked to the religious institutions and shrines named in the order "is listed, hosted, advertised, exhibited, or offered for sale on its platform without verifiable documentary proof of authorization from the concerned institution". Amazon submitted a framework covering 10 major religious institutions and shrines, including Ram Janmabhoomi Mandir, Tirumala Tirupati Devasthanam, Shri Mata Vaishno Devi Shrine, Shri Kashi Vishwanath Temple, Shri Jagannath Temple, Shri Kedarnath Temple, Shri Badrinath Temple, Shri Somnath Temple, Shri Dwarkadhish Temple and Shri Mahakaleshwar Temple. In its 19-page order, the CCPA said the phrase "Shri Ram Mandir Ayodhya Prasad" has a specific and widely understood meaning among Hindu devotees, referring to sacred food offered to and blessed by the deity at the Ram Mandir in Ayodhya. "The commercial appropriation of this phrase for ordinary confectionery products, without any authorisation from the Shri Ram Janmabhoomi Teerth Kshetra Trust, constitutes not just a misleading trade practice under the CP Act but an affront to the religious sentiments of crores of consumers," the CCPA said. The CCPA issued a Show Cause Notice to Amazon on the same day, three days before the Ram Mandir's Pran Pratishtha ceremony on January 22, 2024. The notice cited alleged violations of the Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020 and the Consumer Protection Act, 2019. Amazon removed the listings after receiving the notice. The company stated that it was only an intermediary and was therefore entitled to safe-harbour protection under Section 79 of the Information Technology Act, citing the Supreme Court's judgment in Shreya Singhal v Union

headline: Chennai metro phase-2 inauguration: I feel like a mother watching her child take its first steps, Stalin says
content: Days before the inauguration of the Chennai Metro Rail phase-2 line between Poonamallee and Vadapalani by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, former chief minister M K Stalin said seeing the line open for public use fills him with the satisfaction of "a mother watching her child take its first steps".In an X post, Stalin highlighted the DMKs role in the Chennai metro project, asserting that the party's contribution to Tamil Nadu's infrastructure legacy remains unerasable.Stalin recalled the inauguration of Valluvar Kottam in Chennai in 1976, which former chief minister M Karunanidhi could not attend despite steering its execution. He recalled Karunanidhis iconic words that "The place we earn in history is not obtained through favours! It is a place that cannot be erased, no matter what happens."Emphasising that the DMK govt spearheaded the conceptualisation and early execution of the metro network, Stalin noted that political transitions could not rewrite historical contributions.As the PoonamalleeVadapalani stretch prepares for public operations on Oct 11, he reiterated that every major developmental milestone in Tamil Nadu bears the unmistakable hallmark of the DMK administration, guaranteeing its place in the state's growth narrative regardless of who presides over the ceremonial ribbon-cutting.

headline: India-EU green shipping corridor: Why India could become a major fuel exporter
content: India has the potential to emerge as a major exporter of green fuels as it works with European partners to develop a green shipping corridor linking India with Europe, industry leaders said on Wednesday at Sagarmanthan: The Great Oceans Dialogue 2026 in New Delhi. Speaking during a session on the India-EU Green Shipping Corridor: Innovation, Action and Scale, industry executives said Indias renewable energy potential, growing green-fuel ecosystem and expanding port infrastructure could position the country as a key supplier for the global shipping industrys transition to cleaner fuels. BC Tripathi, Vice Chairman of AM Green, said green fuels produced in India should be exported directly rather than routed through established hubs such as Singapore and Hong Kong. If green fuels are produced in India, why should they be shipped around Singapore or Hong Kong? Now that fuel is being produced in India, why should we not export it directly from India? Tripathi said the India-EU initiative was significant because it was moving beyond discussions on green shipping corridors towards actual implementation, with data and insights emerging from the process. Sudhir Pathak, CTO of Hero Future Energies, said the coalition should help position India as an exporter of green fuels while reducing dependence on imported energy for shipping. We want to shape this coalition so that India becomes the next exporter of green fuels and we are able to deliver shipping with our own fuel, becoming totally independent. Pathak said India could leverage its abundant solar resources and its expertise in converting intermittent renewable power into controlled, round-the-clock energy. The push comes as the global shipping industry faces increasing pressure to reduce emissions. Anupam Sawhney of Sembcorp India said shipping accounts for almost 3% of global greenhouse gas emissions and that stronger regulations would create demand for scalable supplies of green fuels. India is in a leading and unique position to support the transition to green shipping, Sawhney said, pointing to the country's ability to scale renewable energy at competitive costs. The proposed corridor aims to assess the feasibility of an India-Europe green hydrogen and green shipping corridor, potentially creating a supply chain connecting Indian green-fuel producers with European shipping demand. Rajeev Goyal of EXMAR said India has the potential to develop green ammonia and has already demonstrated its ability to transport and burn ammonia. When the manufacturers and the ports are ready, we are ready to ship. Goyal said the company believes the shipping industry will increasingly move towards green fuels and that EXMAR is prepared to support that transition. But industry executives also stressed that producing green fuel alone will not be enough. Ports will need dedicated infrastructure for storing, handling and exporting these fuels. Sudhish Pandey of Aegis Vopak said storage infrastructure at ports would be an integral and critical part of the ecosystem. The company wants to explore shared port infrastructure for the storage, export and movement of green energy and green fuels, he said. Capt. Suraj Sundaresan of Eastern Pacific Shipping said the shipping industry shares the objective of accelerating the transition towards lower-carbon fuels. We need to be as fast as possible off the ground to reduce emissions and move into the low-carbon sector, he said. The emerging India-EU green shipping corridor, therefore, involves more than developing alternative fuels.

headline: Unmanned frontline: From combat to high-risk evacuations, how robots are replacing troops in Russia-Ukraine war
content: Unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs) are emerging as a critical new element of the Russia-Ukraine war, taking on some of the most dangerous frontline tasks as Ukraine tries to offset manpower shortages and reduce soldiers exposure on a battlefield saturated with drones. Ukrainian military units are increasingly deploying four-wheeled and tracked ground robots for combat, logistics, ammunition deliveries and casualty evacuations. The shift is part of a broader effort to use unmanned systems not just in the air, but increasingly on the ground, as the war stretches into its fifth year. Reuters reported from a workshop near the frontline in northeastern Ukraine, where military mechanics were preparing four-wheeled unmanned vehicles known as Hyenas. The robots can carry explosives towards Russian positions and attack enemy dugouts or help halt advancing troops, according to the Reuters report. The development comes as Ukrainian forces seek to preserve manpower along a roughly 1,200-km frontline. Brigadier General Andrii Biletskyi, commander of Ukraines Third Army Corps, described the gradual replacement of infantry with UGVs as the next revolution in warfare, according to Reuters. His corps aims to replace around one-third of its frontline troops with unmanned systems by the end of 2026. Biletskyi said infantry now performs only about 10% of the tasks it carried out before the battlefield became dominated by persistent aerial threats. UGVs are being used to transport ammunition and food to frontline positions and evacuate wounded soldiers from dangerous areas. Reuters reported that Ukrainian forces have integrated unmanned ground systems into units across the front as they seek to reduce the risks faced by troops. Ukraine is also expanding the number and types of ground robotic systems entering military service. In September, Ukrainian company Air3Fs Varkhan ground robotic system was officially codified and approved for use by the countrys defence forces, according to Kyiv-based news publication Ukrainska Pravda, citing the company. The four-wheel-drive Varkhan can reportedly carry up to 300 kg of cargo and travel up to 37 km with that load. Its range increases to 50 km without a load, while its maximum speed is 20 km/h. The company said, as cited in the report, that the system has already been used in combat conditions for frontline logistics missions. The rise of UGVs follows Ukraines rapid development of aerial and maritime drones during the war. That experience has helped create a close feedback loop between Ukraines armed forces and its domestic defence industry. Ukrainian drone makers have developed and modified systems based on battlefield experience, while Russia has simultaneously expanded its own drone capabilities and sought ways to counter Ukrainian systems. The same dynamic is now moving beyond aerial drones to ground robots. The growing use of UGVs points to a battlefield where soldiers increasingly operate alongside and in some roles are replaced by machines. UGVs can carry supplies into dangerous areas, evacuate wounded troops and undertake some high-risk combat missions without directly exposing personnel. But they are not a complete replacement for infantry. Reuters noted that their mobility limitations and production constraints mean human troops will remain essential for many battlefield tasks. The Russia-Ukraine war is therefore becoming a testing ground for a broader model of warfare. The evolution from drone warfare in the skies to unmanned systems across the battlefield could be one of the most significant lessons emerging from the conflict and a glimpse of how future land warfare may increasingly be fought.

headline: Tamil Nadu By-Election Results 2026 Date and Time: How to check Dharapuram, Madurantakam results online

headline: Canada's Anne Carson Awarded 2026 Nobel Prize In Literature For 'Bold And Inventive' Work
content: Nobel laureate Anne Carson is known for works that blur literary genres and push the boundaries between poetry, prose and other art forms. Canadian author Anne Carson was awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature on Thursday for her bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature". When the Nobel Committee called Carson to tell her she had won, she said she was in Iceland, listening to the wind". - Arsonist As Firefighter?: Pakistan Waging Global War Against Terror, Mohsin Naqvi Tells UN Chief - False Information: Russia Rejects Reports Of Second Plague Case After Lab Workers Death - US Lost 81 Aircraft Including F-35s, F-15Es In Iran War; Tehran Mocks Real Toll Is Far Higher - Khalistan Referendum Meets Alberta Independence Vote: Canada Faces New Separatist Challenge | Exclusive Born in Toronto in 1950, Carson has spent her career moving between poetry, translation, classical scholarship and teaching. Her writing repeatedly brings ancient Greek and Roman literature into conversation with modern writers, contemporary experiences and other art forms. The result is a body of work that rarely stays within the boundaries of a conventional poem, novel or essay. Where Classics Meet Contemporary Life Carsons fascination with language began with her study of Classics. She published her doctoral thesis, Odi et Amo Ergo Sum, in 1981 and has since combined poetry with translations of ancient Greek texts and teaching at universities. The etymology of words has been a starting point for much of her work. Her translations of Classical Greek texts have also been treated as literary works in their own right, including her interpretations of fragments by the Greek poet Sappho in If Not, Winter (2002). Canadian author and poet Anne Carson won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature. Carson was informed about the award while she was in Iceland. The 76-year-old writer is known for work that moves between poetry, prose, classical literature, and translation. Carson's best-known works include Autobiography of Red, The Beauty of the Husband, and Wrong Norma. Carson has taught classics and literature at universities including McGill, Princeton, and the University of California, Berkeley. She has also translated Greek tragedies including Sophocles Electra and Antigone and Euripides Bakkhai. But Carson does not simply bring the ancient world into the present. She places ancient writers alongside modern ones, allowing them to speak to and against each other. In Economy of the Unlost (1999), she puts the sixth-century BC Greek poet Simonides of Keos in dialogue with 20th-century poet Paul Celan. In Men in the Off Hours (2000), she brings the Greek historian Thucydides together with Virginia Woolf. Carson has described this approach as a stereoscopic vision" which is holding two perspectives at once". It is a method that allows her to move between centuries, genres and artistic forms while questioning the boundaries between them. The Essay That Set The Tone Carsons 1986 book Eros the Bittersweet established many of the ideas that would shape her later work. The book examines Eros through the poetry of Sappho and the ancient Greek understanding of desire as something simultaneously pleasurable and painful. For Carson, the distance between a lover and the beloved is precisely what gives desire its force. Her writing similarly creates energy by placing different voices and perspectives alongside each other. That tendency would become one of the defining characteristics of her work: the unexpected combination of things that appear, at first, to belong to different worlds. A Poem, A Story, An Emily Bront Reading In The Glass Essay, published in Glass, Irony, and God in 1995, Carson pushed the long poem into territory usually associated with fiction and the essay. The poem follows a woman who, after being left by her husband, visits her mother in the lonely moorlands. She takes with her the works of Emily Bront, whose own landscapes and inner world become woven into the story. The work is simultaneously a poem, a story about abandonment and a reading of Bront. Three lonely women at a kitchen table become the centre of a meditation on grief, love and loss, with Carson allowing the poems shifts in scene and perspective to shape the story. The boundaries between genres begin to disappear. Autobiography Of Red: Greek Myth, Rebuilt Carson took that approach even further in Autobiography of Red: A Novel in Verse, published in 1998. The book takes its inspiration from fragments by the sixth-century BC Greek poet Stesichorus about Geryon, the winged red monster defeated by Heracles. In the classical myth, Geryon is a terrifying giant whose cattle Heracles steals as part of one of his labours. Carson transforms him. Her Geryon is a young, vulnerable character devoted to his mother who falls in love with Heracles. The ancient myth becomes a modern coming-of-age story about desire, abuse, love and the pain of loving someone who may ultimately destroy you. It is perhaps the clearest example of Carsons larger literary method: taking something ancient and allowing it to become startlingly contemporary without abandoning its classical roots. Boredom Is My Arch-Enemy Carson has described boredom as her arch-enemy", and humour is one of the ways she keeps it at bay. In The Beauty of the Husband: A Fictional Essay in 29 Tangos (2001), she turns the breakdown of a marriage into a sharp, sardonic work that moves between poetry and prose. Each of its 29 sections opens with lines from John Keats, whose idealised connection between beauty and truth is placed against the messiness and deception of a failing relationship. Again, Carson takes two apparently incompatible worlds and makes them collide. A Brother, A Box And An Ancient Roman Poem One of Carsons most personal works is Nox, published in 2010 in memory of her brother Michael, who died in Denmark in 2000. Nox is not presented like a conventional book. It takes the form of a box containing an accordion-folded sequence of photographs, letters, fragments and other texts. Running through it is Carsons grief over her brothers death. But even here, the ancient world enters the work. Carson brings in the Roman poet Catullus and his famous elegy for his own dead brother, who also died abroad. Her translation of Catullus poem becomes another voice in the work, connecting her personal grief with an ancient poets experience of mourning. A Book That Can Be Read In Any Order Carsons experimentation has continued throughout her career. Float, published in 2016, consists of 22 chapbooks on different subjects that can be read in any order. Her 2024 work Wrong Norma similarly brings together different kinds of writing and performance, crossing into academic and artistic territory. Carson has also collaborated with visual artists, choreographers and directors working in opera and theatre. The form keeps changing, but the impulse remains familiar: to test what literature can do when it refuses to remain inside its traditional borders. Why Anne Carson Won The Nobel Committees citation describes Carsons work as being in playful dialogue with the classical tradition". That phrase captures much of her literary career. She takes Sappho, Stesichorus, Catullus, Sophocles and other writers from antiquity and places them beside Emily Bront, Virginia Woolf, Paul Celan and contemporary experiences of love, grief and identity. Sometimes the result is a poem that behaves like an essay. Sometimes it is a novel written in verse. Sometimes it is a box of photographs, letters and fragments. Across those forms, Carson has made the ancient world feel contemporary and made contemporary literature look unexpectedly ancient. It is this restless experimentation, the Nobel Committee said, that has helped her create new forms for contemporary literature". Canadian author and poet Anne Carson won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature for her bold and inventive oeuvre that engages with the classical tradition and creates new forms for contemporary literature.

headline: Distribution of medicine in covers with Hindi words printed kicks up a row
content: The covers, which are being distributed to the patients, bear drug consumption details in Tamil, English and Hindi languages, in contravention of the two-language policy of Tamil and English of the State government. The covers contain details on when and how to consume medicines. A few patients, upon noticing the Hindi letters on the covers, have been circulating them on various social media platforms. headline: Who is Anne Carson? Canadian writer and poet wins 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature for her 'bold and inventive oeuvre'
content: Canadian poet and writer Anne Carson, 76, has been awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature "for her bold and inventive oeuvre that, in playful dialogue with the classical tradition, has created new forms for contemporary literature," the Nobel award-giving body announced on Thursday. Ingrid Carlberg, permanent secretary of the Swedish Academy, said the author was in Iceland listening to the wind when the academy contacted her to inform her about the win. The award was announced by the Swedish Academy in Stockholm. The Nobel Prize carries a cash award of 12 million Swedish kronor this year, equivalent to around $1.2 million, whether it is awarded to an individual, a small group of laureates or an organisation. Born in Toronto, Carson frequently draws inspiration from themes and narratives in ancient Greek and Roman literature, with her works often combining poetry, essays and fiction. Her bibliography includes Eros the Bittersweet, which explores desire's pleasure and pain in ancient Greek literature; the verse novel Autobiography of Red; Men in the Off Hours, a poetry and prose collection that received Canada's Griffin Prize for poetry in 2001; and Norma Jeane Baker of Troy, which draws parallels between Marilyn Monroe and Helen of Troy. Carson enrolled at St. Michaels College at the University of Toronto but left the institution twice, at the end of both her first and second years. Unhappy with the limitations of the curriculum, particularly a compulsory course on Milton, she briefly turned to graphic arts. She later returned to the University of Toronto, earning her Bachelor of Arts in 1974, Master of Arts in 1975 and Ph.D. in 1981. Carson also spent a year at the University of St Andrews, where she studied Greek metrics and Greek textual criticism. With an academic background in classics, Carson brings together influences from comparative literature, anthropology, history and the arts in her writing. Her work frequently revisits and reinterprets texts from Ancient Greek and Latin literature, drawing on authors such as Aeschylus, Catullus, Euripides, Homer, Sappho, Sophocles and Thucydides. She also incorporates ideas and influences from a range of modern writers and philosophers, including Emily Bront, Paul Celan, Emily Dickinson, Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel, Martin Heidegger, Friedrich Hlderlin, Franz Kafka, John Keats, Gertrude Stein, Simone Weil and Virginia Woolf. headline: Ajmer jailer took two inmates for housework. Now she's jailed in same prison
content: Living away from her husband, Divya Chaudhary wanted help managing her two young daughters and rented accommodation, about 8 km from the Ajmer Central Jail where she worked as a jailer. Apparently unable to handle the increasing workload at home and office, the 37-year-old came up with an idea: taking the help of two female inmates lodged at the Womens Reformatory within the Central Jail. On July 12, Divya tried to walk out of jail with two inmates Kiran alias Setha, who is serving a life sentence, and Sana, an undertrial. The episode has now put Chaudhary behind bars in the same jail where she was responsible for the custody and security of inmates. Police allege that she misused her position to take the two women out for domestic work, despite protests from jail staff. Under the Rajasthan Prisons Rules, 2022, the jailer (karapal) is responsible for the custody, security and discipline of prisoners and for reporting security lapses and other irregularities to the Superintendent. According to officials, Chaudhary, along with her friend and colleague, constable Sonia Chaudhary, tried to walk out of the jail with the two inmates, but an altercation ensued at the gates. Officials said that despite the protests of other jail personnel posted at the main gate of the womens prison, Chaudhary and Sonia intimidated the staff. A native of Rajasthans Bhilwara, Chaudhary lived on rent in Ajmer, while her husband, also a jailer, was posted in Kota. Her daughters are very young. She wanted them (the inmates) to take care of her daughters and also clean the house, Ajmer Deputy SP Shivam Joshi said. Soon after she left, word spread, and the two inmates stayed out for barely an hour or two before they were back inside, the police said. Her actions were illegal and unlawful; prisoners are kept in jail under the protection of the court. So, a case was lodged, and an investigation was initiated, the DSP said. Once the internal inquiry was completed and her guilt was established, a case was registered at Ajmers Civil Lines police station on August 5 based on a report from Ajmer Central Jail guard Mahipal Mangloda. However, to avoid arrest, Chaudhary went absconding after the FIR was registered. A special police team was formed under Civil Lines SHO Shambhu Singh, under the direction of Additional SP Himanshu Jangid and Deputy SP Shivam Joshi. The team included regular police personnel as well as officials from the cyber cell. The police team thoroughly analysed CCTV footage, technical evidence, and records from the crime scene and began tracking her with the help of the cyber cell. On Tuesday, October 6, a special team of Ajmer police raided a residential flat in Kota district and arrested her, an official said. Moinuddeen, ASI at Ajmers Civil Lines police station, said that she was at her husbands rented apartment. He is a prison guard in Kota. Earlier, both the daughters were with her in Ajmer. We tracked her location with her mobile number Her husband was at his village when we went to the Kota apartment. In her defence, she has claimed that she wanted someone to help clean her house and had asked her subordinate (Sonia) to get women from the Open Jail, as they can step out. But the subordinate brought these two women instead. Of course she will claim innocence now he said. The unusual case had an unusual culmination too; as per DSP Shivam Joshi, She has now been lodged at the same jail she was working at.

headline: Big Relief For Businesses? Faster Registration, ITC And Refunds On GST Council Agenda
content: 57th GST Council meeting is being held, with the measures focused on reducing compliance requirements, increasing automation and making GST process more efficient for businesses. The 57th GST Council meeting in New Delhi on Thursday approved a set of measures aimed at simplifying compliance, speeding up refunds and reducing the working-capital burden on businesses, Money Control reported quoting sources. This would allow low-risk taxpayers to receive approvals with limited intervention from tax officers, the report stated. The move is aimed at making GST-related processes faster and reducing the manual work involved in routine approvals. Refund claims could also be processed more quickly, with faster provisional payouts being considered. The system would use data from customs and banking platforms to reduce the need for manual checks. MSMEs, exporters likely to benefit The measures are expected to particularly benefit micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs), exporters and businesses holding large input tax credit balances. By speeding up ITC processing and refunds, the changes could help businesses unlock working capital that remains tied up in the GST system. The measures approved by the Council are aimed at easing compliance while improving the speed at which businesses can access refunds and other tax-related credits. Small taxpayers, services exports also in focus The GST Council is also considering measures to ease compliance requirements for small taxpayers. Changes to GST rules governing services exports are also being considered. These changes could benefit global capability centres, according to the information available on the proposals. headline: Microfinance shows early recovery signs, but legacy bad loans weigh on sector
content: India's microfinance sector ended financial year 2026 (FY26) with its loan book down 11% to 3.34 trillion, although a 4% sequential increase in the January-March quarter marked the first signs of a turnaround after a prolonged period of stress, according to the Bharat Microfinance Report 2026 released by Sa-Dhan on Thursday. Sa-Dhan is an RBI-appointed self-regulatory organisation (SRO) for microfinance institutions. The report, however, cautioned that the recovery remains tentative. While stress in the current loan book has eased sharply, legacy stressed assets continue to weigh on the sector, with the share of loans overdue by 180 days or more rising to 17.04% in March 2026 from 10.67% a year earlier. The report said the number of loan accounts fell 21% to 10.40 crore at the end of March 2026, from 13.18 crore a year earlier. The contraction in loan accounts, alongside the 11% decline in outstanding credit, reflects the cautious approach adopted by micro-lenders following two years of high credit stress, concerns over household indebtedness and borrowers taking loans from multiple lenders. FY202526 can be characterised as a period of consolidation and recalibration, with lenders focusing on strengthening portfolio quality, controlling borrower indebtedness, improving collections and restoring sustainable credit growth. The third set of guardrails from industry leaders and SROs, issued in April 2026, have strengthened credit discipline. The sectoral outlook is expected to further improve in the current financial year," said Jiji Mammen, executive director and chief executive officer (CEO), Sa-Dhan. At the same time, the report said the rise in outstanding loans in the January-March quarter indicates that new lending has begun to exceed repayments, marking the onset of a fresh growth phase. Asset quality also showed a sharp improvement in the current book. Portfolio at risk (PAR) of 30-179 days past due declined to 2.34% in March 2026 from 6.63% a year earlier, while PAR of 90-179 days stood at 1.45%, down from 3.92%. In microfinance, a loan is typically considered at risk after 30 days of missed payment due to the lack of physical collateral. However, the improvement does not represent a complete resolution of the sectors stress, the report said. PAR of 180 days and above increased to 17.04% from 10.67%, pointing to an ageing pool of legacy defaults even as repayment performance on the current book improved. The portfolio dynamics between March 2026 and March 2025 reveal a clear structural split, the report said, describing a rapid recovery in active repayment behaviour alongside an accumulation of legacy defaulted loans. The report also points to a significant reduction in borrower-level multiple lending. Restrictions limiting borrowers to no more than three micro-lenders and capping total household indebtedness at 2 lakh resulted in 92.6% of unique active borrowers being associated with two or fewer lenders in March 2026, compared with 90.5% a year earlier. More significantly, the share of borrowers associated with five or more lenders fell to 0.1% from 1.6%, suggesting that the tighter lending guardrails have materially reduced high-risk multiple borrowing. The adjustment has been broad-based. Loan accounts declined in 33 states and Union territories, with some of the largest microfinance markets seeing particularly sharp contractions. Karnataka recorded a 28% decline, followed by West Bengal at 24%, Tamil Nadu at 23%, Bihar at 22% and Uttar Pradesh at 17%. The reports assessment of the next phase is more cautious. It said the improvement during FY26 was supported by better harvests, food disinflation, stronger employment and remittances, monetary easing and credit guarantees. These factors helped improve household incomes, funding conditions and portfolio quality. But several of those favourable conditions cannot be assumed to persist, the report cautioned. Inflation has begun rising again, the 2026 monsoon has been below normal in districts with high borrower density and the guarantee facility has expired. Climate variability has emerged as a particularly important medium-term risk because its impact can be simultaneous across borrowers in a district, unlike conventional credit risk, which is generally dispersed across individual borrowers. Through 12 August 2026, cumulative rainfall was 12% below the long-period average, with the eastern and north-eastern regionswhere borrower density is highfacing materially larger shortfalls than the national figure. The report also highlights the uneven financial performance of micro-lenders. Operating cost stood at 8.47% in 2026, up from 7.09% in 2025. Larger institutions demonstrated stronger capacity to absorb costs and generate returns, while several smaller and mid-sized institutions remained under pressure on profitability, return on assets and return

headline: 'False Information': Russia Rejects Reports Of Second Plague Case After Lab Worker's Death
content: Russia has rejected reports of a second pneumonic plague case linked to an Irkutsk anti-plague institute, as WHO seeks clarity over the situation. Russian authorities have denied reports of a second case of pneumonic plague linked to an anti-plague research institute in Siberia, calling the claims circulating on social media false. The Russian state-run TASS news agency, citing the press service of the relevant authorities, reported that information about a second person contracting pneumonic plague was untrue. - Russia Plague Scare: WHO Seeks Answers Over Second Suspected Case As Authorities Call Reports False Information - Russian Lab Worker Dies After Suspected Pathogen Leak: Have Research Accidents Caused Outbreaks Before? - Lab Workers Mysterious Death At Russias Anti-Plague Institute: Why Has It Drawn US Attention? - US Embassy Issues Health Alert, Warns Americans To 'Have A Plan To Depart' Amid Plague Scare In Russia The claim had suggested that an individual who came into contact with an employee of the Irkutsk anti-plague institute had subsequently developed the disease. The clarification comes amid international concern over the death of a 28-year-old laboratory worker, Darya Shipilova, who had been associated with the Irkutsk anti-plague institute. Death Of Lab Worker Raises Concerns Russian authorities have maintained that Shipilova did not die from plague. Officials said she died from pneumonia of unknown aetiology, while post-mortem examinations found no evidence of an infection connected to her professional work. Local media reports had earlier suggested that she may have been exposed to plague after a test tube broke inside the laboratory. The reports have not been independently confirmed. The incident has nevertheless prompted concern over a possible infectious disease outbreak, particularly because of reports that people who may have come into contact with the affected individuals were placed under observation or isolation. The World Health Organization has also been in contact with Russian authorities over the situation. WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus had urged Moscow to clarify media reports concerning a second employee from the institute who was suffering from pneumonia of undetermined cause. WHO Seeks Clarification As Russia Says Situation Is Stable Russias consumer health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor said the situation in the Irkutsk region remained stable. Authorities said nearly 5,000 tests had been carried out and none had detected dangerous pathogens. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov also dismissed reports surrounding a possible second case, saying that much of the information being circulated by the media was false. Despite the official reassurances, uncertainty has fuelled rumours in Shelekhov, the town where the affected institute is located. Residents told AFP that a lack of clear information had contributed to anxiety and confusion. One resident, who was in hospital for observation when a woman died there last week, said patients were temporarily prevented from entering or leaving the facility. Another resident said her relative working at the anti-plague institute had been quarantined. Residents Seek More Information While the town remained outwardly calm, residents expressed concern about how the suspected infection could spread and how it was being detected. Authorities have introduced precautionary measures, including contact tracing and restrictions around the hospital where the woman had been treated. Schools have also reportedly introduced mask requirements in some cases. US President Donald Trump has offered to assist Russia and said he would speak with Russian President Vladimir Putin about the reports. For now, however, Russian authorities continue to reject claims of a second pneumonic plague case, while international health officials are seeking greater clarity over the circumstances surrounding the deaths and illnesses linked to the Irkutsk institute. Russian authorities denied reports of a second case of pneumonic plague linked to the Irkutsk research institute, dismissing the social media claims as false. State-run TASS and Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov confirmed that the information regarding a second infected individual was untrue.

headline: BJP slams TVK-led govt. over sexual assault on five-year-old in Gummidipoondi
content: BJP State unit president Nainar Nagenthran on Thursday (October 8, 2026) criticised the TVK-led government and the Tamil Nadu police over a reported incident of sexual assault on a five-year-old child in Gummidipoondi. He wanted the State to ensure that those involved in the Gummidipoondi offence were punished.

headline: Death toll from Russian bus strike in eastern Ukraine jumps to 30: authorities
